rv.q: But they surely deserve to be articulated with more dramatic force than this.
Its performers bring conviction to challenging material, but too often the intellectual argument elbows the human drama out of the way.
Oftentimes, the musical interludes, much like the wandering prose, become too much like free jazz for a narrative medium.
What emerges is an abstraction of something that is, admittedly, hard in more ways than one to envisage.
The show can feel static and lacking depth, but it is an important glimpse of a cruel, traumatic series of events that should never have happened...

Mai Weisz is outstanding as Arendt, a woman who refused to submit, as indeed she did all her life, to things that had gone wrong, but it is very much an ensemble piece with the players complementing one another.
The Banality of Evil throughout its straight-through 90 minutes is enthralling, engrossing, emotionally exhausting. Above all it's a darkly theatrical must-see.
This is serious theatre, well researched, beautifully performed and choreographed, re-telling an aspect of a story that has been told many times in many ways since the 1940s.
The scenes are punchy, engaging and bring together the women’s stories.
Pascal grants her characters immortality in a play that is the antithesis of banal.
In The Banality of Evil Pascal successfully breathes life into a neglected chapter of history.
Yet dramatically Pascal's work is most potent when embracing good old-fashioned realism.
The physical theatre and use of props create simple yet captivating images, with some genuinely beautiful moments of movement.
The drama is disjointed and short of describing - in sometimes prurient detail - the appalling and inhumane degradation of life in Gurs, says little else, least of all about Arendt.
Instead, it feels like a mash-up driven at a relentlessly tight pace with little breathing space, leaving little to linger in either the mind or the heart.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this stylized drama about Hannah Arendt's internment at Camp Gurs. While some praise the visceral performances and important historical subject matter, others find the theatrical approach uneven and stiff.
